title: The common good
hook: the aims of the law: protect religion, life, mind, lineage and property

segments.voice: Yesterday, 'aql, and your line: reason as a source. When you followed a commitment one link back, what did you find it needed from you? Day one thousand one hundred seventy-four.

Pork is forbidden in the Qur'an. So is meat from an animal that died on its own. And then, in the very same passage of Surah al-Baqarah, comes an exception: whoever is driven by necessity, not wanting it and not going beyond the limit, carries no sin. A person starving in the desert with nothing else to eat is not breaking the law by eating. The rule bends, and the text itself bends it. Why would a law make room against its own prohibition? Because, jurists say, the law has aims, and keeping a person alive is one of them. Today's word is the good those aims protect.
screen: `FORBIDDEN FOOD.` → `UNLESS YOU'RE STARVING.` → `WHY WOULD THE LAW BEND?`

segments.voice: The word is maslahah, benefit, welfare, the good of a thing. Muslim jurists asked a large question with it: what is the law for? The scholar al-Ghazali, in his book on legal theory called al-Mustasfa, gave an answer that later writers took up. The law, he wrote, aims to protect five things for people: their religion, their life, their mind, their lineage, and their property. Whatever protects those, he called maslahah. Whatever harms them, its opposite. Run the five through some familiar rules. Prayer and fasting guard religion. The law of retaliation for killing guards life. The ban on intoxicants guards the mind. The rules of marriage guard lineage, who belongs to whom. The penalty for theft guards property. Each rule has a job. And the jobs explain the exceptions. That's why the starving person may eat: a food rule gives way when life itself is at stake. The Qur'an puts the spirit plainly, in Surah al-Baqarah: "Allah desireth for you ease; He desireth not hardship for you." Later, the Andalusian scholar al-Shatibi, of the Maliki school, built a whole study on these aims, the maqasid. Now the honest part. The schools agree that the law serves people's good. They differ on how far maslahah can go on its own, where no text speaks at all. The Maliki school is known for using it more freely. Others insist it must stay tied to a text, so that nobody's private sense of the common good starts writing law. Even the argument is about protecting the same five things.
screen: `MASLAHAH: THE GOOD OF A THING.` · `FIVE THINGS THE LAW PROTECTS.` · `THE AIMS EXPLAIN THE EXCEPTIONS.` · `HOW FAR CAN IT GO ALONE?`

segments.voice: The practice: name how one rule protects life. Choose any rule you live under, religious or not. A speed limit near a school. Not leaving a child alone near water. Fasting rules that let the sick eat. Hold it in mind and trace it to a life it keeps safe, a real one, a face if you can. Then let the rule look a little less like a fence and a little more like a hand. If you pray, you can give thanks for the lives kept. If not, just rest with that face. The bell holds the time.
Maslahah. Benefit, the common good: what the law's aims protect, religion, life, mind, lineage and property. Today's word.
Your line: the aims of the law. Today, when a rule annoys you, ask which of the five it might be guarding before you decide it's pointless. Day one thousand one hundred seventy-four.

howItsDone: Muslim jurists and teachers often explain rulings by the aims of the law, the protection of religion, life, mind, lineage and property, and the schools differ on how far the common good can be used where no text speaks.

fork.setup: you're lost in the desert, starving, and the only food is meat the Qur'an forbids. what does the passage say?
options: eat, and the sin is forgiven later.
eat: whoever is driven by necessity carries no sin.
don't eat: the rule never bends.
fork.reveal: the text itself makes the exception, for one not wanting it and not going beyond the limit. keeping a life is one of the law's aims.
